Wallet-based key generation now requires one standard signature from the
connected EOA, and contract accounts are routed to manual seedphrase setup.

  results are discarded. Bytecode is read on the wallet's own chain.
- smartWallets: only the exact 23-byte EIP-7702 designator counts as an EOA;
  a failed read returns 'Unknown'.
- Welcome and Menu share an allowlist (Standard EOA, EIP-7702) and show a
  message when a wallet cannot be used or the check is still pending.

Merge pull request #249 from 0xbow-io/fix/dev-241-usdt-allowance-reset

fix(deposit): zero a leftover allowance before approving USDT

fix(deposit): Safe batches always zero the allowance first

A multi-sig Safe transaction can execute long after it is proposed, so
the allowance read at proposal time cannot decide whether USDT needs the
reset. The Safe batch now always approves 0 before the amount; approve(0)
never reverts.

The Safe Apps hook and utils/safe.ts built the same batch twice and only
the unused copy was tested. Both now come from buildSafeApprovalDepositTxs,
which the tests cover.

buildApprovalCalls returns no call when the known allowance already
covers the amount, instead of an approve that USDT would reject.

fix(deposit): zero a leftover allowance before approving USDT

USDT on Ethereum reverts approve() when it moves a non-zero allowance to
another non-zero value. A partial allowance left by an approval whose
deposit never ran (rejected signature, failed simulation) then blocked
every later, larger USDT deposit: the approve reverted in the standard
flow and the whole batch failed in the 7702 and Safe flows.

When the current allowance is non-zero but below the deposit, approve 0
first. The standard flow sends it as its own transaction, the batch
flows prepend it as a call. The 7702 path now takes the deposit from the
last receipt whatever the call count.

refactor(units): name the pool-units rule once, and test that instead

Build and Test was red on three suites I added, and the reason was the level
they worked at rather than anything they claimed. To assert which decimals a
pool amount uses they rendered a provider, a table, a review section and a
success screen, which drags in packages jest does not transform
(@mui/icons-material, then @vanilla-extract/sprinkles). They passed under bun
and failed under node, and I kept verifying against the wrong runner.

The rule they were testing was worth naming anyway. It was the same expression
written out at NINETEEN call sites, and the defect this all started from was
that fifteen of them had it backwards: they took the decimals from
`balanceBN`, wagmi's useBalance for the CONNECTED WALLET, whose placeholder
says 18 for everything while the query is unresolved.

`poolDecimals` and `poolSymbol` in src/utils/poolUnits.ts are that rule, pure
and dependency-free, and every site now calls them. Same behaviour, one
definition, and a rule with no imports needs no rendering to test.

The new suite covers what the three did plus what they did not: that a resolved
wallet balance disagreeing does not move a pool amount, that a 0-decimal asset
survives (`||` would have dropped it), and that the number and the label come
from the same source, which is the property whose absence produced "5388570
divided by 1e18, labelled USDC".

Verified under CI's runner this time, not bun: 25 suites, 268 tests, 0 failures.
That is the whole suite green, including the four that fail under bun locally.
eslint 0 errors, tsc at its 88 baseline, prettier clean.

fix(test): load mocked modules in a hook both runners support

Third attempt at the same CI failure, so the reason is worth writing down.

These three suites must load their modules AFTER the jest.mock calls beside
them, because a static import is hoisted above those and would capture the real
modules. The two obvious ways to do that each work in exactly one of the two
environments:

  - `require` does not exist under the ESM jest CI runs. It worked here only
    because bun provides one.
  - top-level `await import` is not supported by the transform used locally.

So neither local green nor CI green meant the other. A dynamic import inside an
async `beforeAll` is the one form both accept, with the bindings declared above
it and assigned there.

The `~/` alias mapping from the previous commit stays: it fixed a real second
problem, that a relative path resolved from a different base in each runner.

251 pass locally with only the four suites that were already failing before
today. eslint 0 errors, tsc at 88, prettier clean.

fix(test): mocked module paths resolve the same way in CI as they do here

The three regression suites added with the decimals fix passed locally and
failed in CI with "Cannot find module '../config' from 'jest.setup.ts'". That
turned Build and Test red from 40a2a03 onward; it was green on the two commits
before it, so this is mine and not pre-existing.

`jest.mock` calls are hoisted and resolved before next/jest applies the tsconfig
alias, so the paths had to be relative. Relative to WHAT then differed between
the two runners: here they resolved from the test file, in CI from jest.setup.ts.
The suites were not wrong, the question "relative to what" was.

Mapping `~/` explicitly in jest.config.ts removes the question. The suites use
the alias the rest of the codebase already uses, and it resolves absolutely
under both runners.

Worth noting for anyone who reads the counts: CI ran 260 tests with 0 failures
while showing this red, because a suite that fails to COMPILE reports no
failing tests at all. The passing count was never the thing to look at.

Locally: 251 pass, and the only failing suites are the four that were already
failing before any of today's work (accountProvider, auth, dataService,
useRequestQuote). eslint 0 errors, tsc at its 88 baseline, prettier clean.

perf(rpc): a custom endpoint scans 500k blocks unless it is known to refuse

QA loaded one account in about twenty minutes on an endpoint that was answering
perfectly. Discovery is thousands of `eth_getLogs`, and the range was 10,000
blocks each.

10,000 was the SDK's own default and it is SAFE rather than good: it is what a
rate-limiting hosted provider tolerates, so everyone paid for the endpoints
that cap low. The default is now 500,000, which is what a node or gateway you
control actually serves (measured on Tenderly, which is what QA was using).

The providers that genuinely refuse a large range keep 10,000, by name.
`defaultChunkForEndpoint` gives Alchemy, Ankr and dRPC the careful number and
everything else the large one, because anything we do not recognise is almost
certainly a node, a gateway or a proxy the user runs. DAppNode is recognised
AS a node, so it gets 500,000.

Getting this wrong in the other direction is worse than slow: too large a range
makes the event scan die and the account load with no pools and no balances. So
the warning is now by PROVIDER first and size second. A blanket threshold was
the only signal before, and at a 500,000 default it would have fired on the
default itself, which teaches people to ignore it. If a recognised low-cap
endpoint is in the form and the range is above 10,000, it says which provider
and what will happen.

The test that pinned the old default is updated rather than deleted: it
recorded a decision, and the decision changed. It now records the new one and
why, and asserts the property that matters, that the shipped default does not
warn about itself.

251 tests pass, tsc at its 88 baseline, eslint 0 errors, prettier clean.

fix(lint): the new tests pass the lint the build runs

The Vercel build runs `pnpm run lint:fix` before `next build`, and that lints
`src/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}`, tests included. The three regression suites added
with the decimals fix failed it, so the deploy stopped before compiling. I ran
jest, tsc and prettier and did not run eslint, which is the one gate the build
itself runs.

The `require` calls stay and the rule is disabled for exactly those lines, with
the reason written down: a static import is hoisted above the `jest.mock` calls
beside it, so the real modules would be captured before the mocks are installed
and the suites would exercise the real ones. Load order is the point.

`createElement(ChainProvider, { children })` becomes
`createElement(ChainProvider, null, children)`, which is the actual React API
rather than a lint appeasement, and one import-order autofix.

246 tests still pass, tsc unchanged at its 88 baseline, prettier clean, and
eslint now reports 0 errors with only the pre-existing useRequestQuote warning.

fix(units): pool amounts use the pool's decimals, never the wallet query's

QA could not withdraw: Confirm failed with a generic error and the console said
"Error in template Num2Bits_217 / Withdraw_219", a range check inside the
circuit.

`balanceBN` is wagmi's useBalance for the CONNECTED WALLET, and while that
query is unresolved the provider substituted a placeholder that claimed 18
decimals for every asset. A dozen consumers read those decimals as though they
described the POOL asset. For 6-decimal USDC during that window:

  - the pool account rendered as "<0.001 USDC", still labelled USDC
  - Review showed "Remaining in Pool Account: -5.38856999999461143 USDC"
  - the proof was asked for 5388570000000000000 out of a commitment worth
    5388570, which the circuit refused as out of range

That last one is the failure QA hit. The screen said nothing useful because
every figure on it was self-consistently wrong.

The placeholder now carries the selected pool's decimals and symbol, and each
consumer takes `selectedPoolInfo.assetDecimals` directly rather than trusting
it. Both halves matter: the placeholder stops being wrong, and no screen
depends on it being right.

REVIEWED BY CODEX (gpt-6-astra), which found eleven more consumers than the
four this started as, two of them P1:

  - Review.tsx: the relayer quote and the SIGNED FEE COMMITMENT parsed the
    withdrawal with wallet decimals, so the quoted amount was 10^12 times the
    commitment amount.
  - DataSection.tsx: a second, independent quote consumer doing the same.
  - useDeposit.ts: deposit transaction values and ERC-20 allowance comparisons.

It also read symbol() and decimals() over RPC for all 25 configured pools
rather than trusting the config. Every decimals matches. Four symbols do not
(wBTC/WBTC, WOETH/wOETH, BSCUSD/USDT, WETH/ETH), so pool screens now show the
configured label consistently while the wallet menu keeps the wallet's own
spelling, which is what that one is about.

Native gas keeps its own 18 decimals in FeeBreakdown. Using pool decimals there
would have been the same bug pointing the other way.

19 regression tests, including the real useWithdraw proof-input call at 6, 8
and 18 decimals and after a pool change. 246 pass, up from 227, with the same
four pre-existing suite failures. tsc unchanged at its 88 baseline.

fix(rpc): a chain with no endpoint of the user's own is not queried

The app discovers notes across every chain it knows about, and the override is
per chain, so filling one field left every other chain's queries going to our
proxy. Someone who set an endpoint to stop routing through us was still routing
through us for all but one network, and nothing on screen said so.

Set none and nothing changes: we serve everything, as before. Set ONE and the
rule flips, because at that point the user has expressed a preference and
quietly ignoring it for the other twenty networks is the wrong way to be wrong.
Chains without an endpoint drop out of discovery rather than falling back.

That has a real cost and it is deliberate: notes on a skipped chain stop
appearing until an endpoint is set for it. So the form names those chains while
the user is still typing, above the test row and below the prefill button that
fills them in one click, and says plainly that funds there will not show.
Clearing every endpoint restores the old behaviour.

queryableChainIds and skippedChainIds are pure and take the map rather than
reading it, so the query path and the warning cannot disagree about which
chains are in play. A test pins them as exact complements for any input, which
is the property that keeps the warning honest.

feat(rpc): reach the custom RPC form before signing in

The form lived only in the account menu, and Header renders that menu only
once there is a wallet or a session. So the one setting that decides whether
signing in works at all could only be changed after signing in. On a slow
endpoint that means waiting out the load before you are allowed to touch the
thing causing it; on a dead one there is no way through (Mike, 2026-09-22: "we
must enable users to select custom rpc before logging in").

Signed out, a globe button sits beside Connect and opens the same modal.
Signed in, the menu item still covers it and the button is not rendered, so
there is never more than one way in on screen at once.

Nothing else had to move: Modals mounts unconditionally in app/layout, and the
form reads no session, no account and no address. It was only ever the door
that was behind the lock.

The button colours itself once an endpoint is in force, so someone who set one
on an earlier visit can see that from the header instead of opening the form to
check. That state is read in an effect rather than during render, because it
comes from localStorage and a value read during render would make the first
client paint disagree with the server markup.

fix(modal): a modal taller than the window can be scrolled to its buttons

The grid made the custom RPC form shorter. It never made it BOUNDED, and that
is the half that stranded QA: ModalContainer had no max height and no overflow,
and SModal is `position: fixed` and centred, so a box that outgrows the viewport
hangs off both edges with nothing able to scroll it. Not the box, which had no
overflow. Not the page behind, which a fixed overlay does not move. Whatever sat
at the bottom, which in a form is the button you came to press, could not be
reached at any window height below the form's own. Making the browser window
smaller was the only way through (Mike, 2026-09-22).

The shell now caps at `calc(100dvh - 2.4rem)` and hides its overflow, and a new
ModalScroll inside it does the scrolling. They are separate so the close button,
which is positioned against the shell, stays put instead of sliding away with
the content. `minHeight: 0` on the scroller is what makes the cap hold: without
it a flex child refuses to shrink below its content and the overflow returns.

`justifyContent: flex-start` on the scroller, because centring pushes the first
rows off the TOP once content overflows, where no scroll reaches them. It looks
identical when the modal fits, since the box is sized by its content.

No scrollbar is drawn. Wheel, trackpad, touch drag, keyboard and find-on-page
all still move it, and `overscrollBehavior: contain` stops a flick at the end of
the list from scrolling the page underneath on a phone.

It sits in BaseModal rather than in the one form because every modal has this
shape and none of them benefits from running off the screen. On a modal that
fits, all of it is inert.

fix(rpc): say that a free endpoint means a slow first load

A free public endpoint ANSWERS, so every field in the form goes green and the
whole thing looks healthy, and then the account takes about twenty minutes to
appear. Discovery is thousands of queries and a public gateway rate limits them
(-32005). Nothing is broken and nothing looks broken, which is the worst shape
a wait can have.

QA sat through the full twenty minutes on a public gateway before working out
it was the endpoint, and asked for the line (Mike, 2026-09-22). It goes above
the fields rather than with the other notes below them, because it changes
which endpoint someone picks rather than explaining one they have already
entered.
Add Claude Code GitHub Workflow (#245)
"Claude Code Review workflow"

fix: the five findings from the review on #243

relayedReceipt, a successful withdrawal reported as reverted: blocks and
logs are served by different nodes and the log node routinely lags, so a
block could list the transaction while the logs for it came back empty.
That was read as a revert and the user was told their funds had not
moved, on a withdrawal that went through. A revert now has to be seen
twice, a poll apart, with the logs for that exact block re-read in
between. A real revert costs one extra interval.

relayedReceipt, one flaky response killing the wait: nothing in the loop
was guarded, so a single 429 or dropped socket threw, the UI fell back to
the withdraw modal, and the fee and withdrawal were never recorded while
the transaction landed anyway. Every read is now attempted and a failure
just waits for the next poll; only the budget ends it. The cursor
advances only past blocks actually read, so a failed range is re-read
rather than skipped.

customRpc, the blocks-per-request setting saved to the store being
vacated: the chunk was written before the URLs moved, without naming a
store, so it resolved to wherever the URLs still were. The reader then
followed the URLs to the new store, found nothing, and fell back to
10,000-block ranges, which is exactly the failure the field exists to
prevent. setCustomRpcChunk now takes the persistence and clears the other
store, and the modal passes the same value it passes for the URLs.

customRpc, the toast shown to users who never set an endpoint: the filter
read a missing chainId as "mine", and the SDK's error objects carry no
chainId, so every error passed. An entry that names no chain now counts
only when the user has a custom endpoint at all.

Menu, the recovery phrase disappearing: a seed-only sign-up that later
connected a wallet matched neither download path and had to disconnect to
get its own phrase back. Holding the seed is the whole condition.

fix(rpc): the custom RPC form fits the screen

One full-width field per network in a single column made the dialog
taller than the viewport with five networks: the save button sat below
the fold and the whole thing read as a narrow ribbon down the middle of
the page.

The endpoints move into a grid that fits as many columns as the width
allows, with a 26rem floor so a phone still gets one. The modal takes
the large size, which is what gives that grid room for more than one
column. Blocks per request is capped at one field width instead of
spanning the dialog, and Save sits beside Use the default RPCs, wrapping
back to a stack when there is no room rather than at a breakpoint that
would have to be kept in sync.

No behaviour change: same fields, same validation, same test ids.

fix(requests): anchor block timestamps for chains scanned through a custom endpoint

A custom RPC replaces sdkRpcUrl too, so its eth_getLogs rows never pass
the proxy that completes blockTimestamp, and a plain node does not return
the field. The registry ended the scan with no dated block for that chain,
estimateBlockTimestamp had nothing to interpolate between, and every
activity date rendered "-".

utils/blockAnchors.ts records blocks the chain picks: head, the earliest
pool deployment block, then midpoints by bisection while a span is longer
than 7 days or its midpoint is more than 120 s off the line between its
ends. Breadth first, one request at a time, at most 500, fail-open. Runs
alongside the event scan for chains with a custom endpoint only, with a
10 s grace after the scan; chains on the proxy issue nothing extra.

Measured against public nodes: slot-time extrapolation from head alone
was hours off on mainnet and years off on BSC (block time changed twice),
so deep anchors are fetched rather than assumed. With the walk, mainnet
dates land within ~2 minutes (399 requests, median error 12 s); a chain
with a fixed block time interpolates exactly.

noTargetedReads: allow-list the new file for .getBlock( (fixed arguments,
none from an event), and pin wagmi's useBalance gate on address so the
recovery-phrase session (no address) issues no balance read.

feat(withdraw): price freshness countdown on the review step

The review step counts down again. Since the split there is no signed
commitment while the user reads, so the countdown is now a client-side
freshness window on the phase-1 price: 60 s from the moment the price is
stored (PRICE_FRESHNESS_WINDOW_MS in utils/priceFreshness, matching the
relayer's commitment window so the number is the familiar one).

At zero nothing is requested. The fee figure is dimmed, the row reads
"Out of date", and a "Refresh price" button appears; clicking it runs
phase 1 once (through fetchPriceWithFallback) and restarts the window. The
clock only writes state; the one request tied to this screen is still the
one made when it opens, plus what the user clicks.

Confirm stays enabled while the price is stale. Phase 2 re-prices and refuses
to commit a fee above the one shown, writing the new figure and asking for a
second click, so an aged figure cannot lead to an overcharge and the step
cannot dead-end the way the old expired-quote screen could. A fee-increased
outcome also restarts the window for the new figure.

The countdown state is shared with the commitment's: the timer counts the
commitment window once Confirm has produced one (between Confirm and
relay), otherwise the price window. Only the commitment case notifies at
zero. QuoteTimer, FlashingExpiredTimer and PulsingButton return as they
were, with the label changed to "Price valid for".

Tests (real hook + context under fake timers, the utils barrel narrowed to
calculateRemainingTime because it pulls wallet UI packages jest cannot
load): the window starts at 60 when the price is stored and counts down;
stale at zero with the fetch mock's call count unchanged after six windows
of elapsed time; Confirm's gate (isPriceCurrent) still true while stale and
commitQuote still commits; a higher phase-2 fee while stale is refused,
shown and given a fresh window; the refresh issues exactly one recipient-free
request and restarts the window.

fix(requests): complete blockTimestamp on eth_getLogs rows at the proxy, derive the rest

67f16e6 dated events from the `blockTimestamp` field on the hypersync proxy's
`eth_getLogs` rows. Measured against production that field is present on 37-51%
of rows only (0x1500000-0x1580000: 996 of 2672 rows; the pool's full mainnet
history, three SDK chunks: 12958 of 25347). The proxy passes the response
through untouched: the upstream RPC returns the same 37% for the same request.
Every row of a block is dated or none is, and the set of dated blocks changes
with the request window, so it is a property of how the upstream pages a range,
not of the block. The same block asked for alone comes back dated.

The hypersync query API joins block `number` + `timestamp` for every block that
holds a matching log. `utils/logTimestampFill.ts`: after an `eth_getLogs` the
proxy runs that query over the same range and address (plus topics when the
request had them), in 128k-block sub-ranges following `next_block`, four at a
time under a 20 s budget, and copies the timestamp onto each undated row. The
requests leaving the proxy are still a function of the range and the pool
address. Fail-open: an error or the deadline leaves the rows as the RPC gave
them. Measured through the route locally with the production key: 25347 of
25347 rows dated over the full history; 996 values the RPC also dated agree.
The 1.5M-block first chunk took 9.6 s against 9.1 s without the fill.

`utils/blockTimestamps.ts` gains a third, DERIVED source for a block neither
the scan nor the session knows: linear between the two nearest recorded blocks
of the chain, else along the chain's mean block time over the recorded span,
capped at now, only with two or more anchors. `resolveEventTimestampSource`
names the source; `resolveAccountTimestamps` counts `estimated` apart. Holding
each of the 512 dated blocks in the probe range out and deriving it from its
neighbours: median error 7 s, p99 60 s, max 213 s. No request either way.

`logTimestampFill.test.ts` pins the filter translation, the exclusive
`to_block`, paging, concurrency, fail-open and the no-request cases;
`blockTimestamps.test.ts` covers the derivation and the source ordering.

feat(auth): sign in with a recovery phrase, no wallet required

The account routes were gated on a connected wallet and login() required
an address, so the manual create/load flows were only reachable after a
wallet connect. Split the one flag in two: hasWallet (wagmi address, for

fix(withdraw): send the recipient at review to relayers that require it

Not every deployed relayer prices a /quote body without a recipient. Probed
2026-09-21: Fast Relay and the testnet relayer answer 200 with the price and
no feeCommitment; Cloaked Relay (Fastify) answers 400
"body must have required property 'recipient'". With the two-phase quote as
pushed, a user on Cloaked Relay got "Failed to get quote" on Review and could
not withdraw.

Phase 1 still goes out without the recipient. If the relayer answers with a
400/422 whose body names `recipient`, the request is retried once with the
recipient and that relayer URL is remembered for the page session, so later
re-prices cost one request. A 400 that does not name the field (asset not
supported, extra gas unavailable) is not retried: those come from the
pricing itself.

For such a relayer the recipient is sent at review time as it was before the
split, so the two-phase behaviour applies to the relayers that price without
it (Fast Relay, testnet) and not to Cloaked Relay. A commitment returned by
the fallback request is dropped: Confirm always runs phase 2 with the
recipient, so one code path signs the fee the user is charged and the 60 s
clock still starts at Confirm for every relayer. The relayer signs one
commitment that is never relayed.

relayerClient.fetchQuote now throws RelayerRequestError carrying the status
and body (same message as before) so the signal is read from the answer, not
from prose in the message.

Tests: the signal on the recorded Fastify body, a 422 naming the field, and
rejections for an asset-unsupported 400, a 500 and a network error; the
retry-and-remember path (no commitment kept), the remembered path, no retry
on an unrelated 400, the retry failing, and phase 2 still sending the
recipient after the fallback; the client error keeps status and body.

fix(withdraw): quote the price on review, the fee commitment on confirm

The relayer's /quote endpoint prices a withdrawal from chain, asset, amount,
extraGas and the live gas price; it only signs a fee commitment (and starts
its 60 s clock) when the body carries a recipient. Until now the review step
sent one request with both amount and recipient, so the recipient went out
for every withdrawal a user merely reviewed and the clock ran while they read
the screen.

The request is now made in two phases against the same relayer:

- Review opens: chain, asset, amount, extraGas, no recipient. The exact fee
  is shown from the returned feeBPS as before. No commitment, no clock.
- Confirm: the same fields plus the recipient. The signed commitment comes
  back and proving starts right away, so the 60 s clock is spent on proving
  and relaying, not on reading.

If the fee in phase 2 is equal to or below the shown one it is committed
(the user pays at most what they saw; the lower number is put on screen). If
it is above, nothing is committed: the new fee is shown and Confirm is
enabled again for a second, informed click. A relayer error in phase 2 leaves
the user on Review with the error; nothing has been proved or relayed.

Confirm is enabled on a current price instead of a commitment. The
"Quote expires" row and the "Request new quote" button leave the review step,
since no clock runs on it anymore. The fee commitment and feeBPSForWithdraw
are set by the Confirm click rather than by a DataSection effect, so the
proof is built from the same feeBPS the relayer signed.

Exits and deposits do not use quotes and are unchanged.

Tests: phase-1 body carries no recipient key (at the request-builder level
and on the wire), phase-2 body carries it, and the equal / lower / higher fee
outcomes.

fix(chain): wallet balance polls on one fixed cadence

The wallet balance read in ChainProvider refetched every 10 s with React
Query's defaults, which also refetch when the window regains focus and
pause the interval while the tab is hidden, so the request timing followed
tab focus. It now polls every 30 s (the v2 app's cadence) with the focus,
background and reconnect refetches switched off: the interval is the only
trigger.

The value is read by Menu (display) and DepositForm (the "Insufficient
balance" check and Max). A whole-balance spend shows the pre-spend figure
for at most one interval; the wallet rejects an over-spend at signing, so
the window costs a retry, not funds.

noTargetedReads.test.ts gains a rule that every refetchInterval is a
literal, and pins the useBalance options.

The relayer quote still fires when the Review step opens. The relayer
signs a commitment for 60 s and rejects it at relay time once expired, and
the proof binds its withdrawalData, so the quote has to precede proving.

refactor(requests): date events from the bulk scan, confirm relays from block data

Two request patterns removed from the login and withdraw paths.

Login used to fetch a block per deposit to date it. The hypersync proxy
already returns `blockTimestamp` on every `eth_getLogs` row and viem's
`formatLog` keeps unknown fields, so the SDK's own bulk scan carries every
timestamp and only drops it when typing events. `utils/dataService.ts` wraps
the SDK's log fetch and records blockNumber -> timestamp per chain as the scan
runs; the account model, the legacy migration and the declined-legacy path all
date from that registry. No extra requests, and the same stream for every user
of a pool. Unknown dates render `-`. The same wrapper also scans withdrawals
from deployment rather than from the user's first deposit block.

Confirming a relay used to poll the relayed hash. `utils/relayedReceipt.ts`
walks new blocks instead: `eth_blockNumber`, `eth_getLogs` by pool and

`WithdrawalRelayed` log decoded at confirmation, and `trace_transaction` is
gone. Receipt polls for our own wallet's transactions are unchanged.

`dataService.test.ts` pins the SDK 1.4.0 internals the capture relies on.

Downstream callers expecting a number (e.g. getUsdBalance, which calls price.toFixed(decimals)) threw silently and fell into a catch that returns '0', so the withdraw review modal rendered '$0.00 USD' for tokens that Alchemy does list (USDS, USDC, etc).

fix: keep Fast Relay as default and fall back to ASP-derived USD price

Two related fixes for the withdraw flow on multi-relayer chains.

Relayer auto-select race: the effect that picks a relayer once fee
queries resolve was firing on every query update. When a faster
secondary relayer (e.g. Cloaked) responded first, it became firstAvailable
while Fast Relay was still loading (isSelectable: false), so the effect
switched the selection to Cloaked. By the time Fast Relay finished, the
effect saw a 'valid current selection' (Cloaked) and bailed out. Net
result: the user never saw Fast Relay as the default. Wait until every
relayer query has finished before doing the auto-select so the first in
configured order wins.

Derived USD price fallback: the review modal (and a few other surfaces)
read price from ChainContext directly. When Alchemy doesn't list a token
or returns 0, the modal renders 'Total Withdrawn 50 USDS / $0.00'. The
PoolPage already worked around this by deriving a per-token price from
the ASP pool stats (acceptedDepositsValueUsd / acceptedDepositsValue).
Move that derivation into ChainProvider so every consumer of
useChainContext().price gets the fallback automatically. This also gives
accurate prices for yield-bearing tokens like sUSDS instead of pinning
them at $1.

fix: use standalone secret derivation for migration proof generation (#14)

## Summary

- Fix migration proof generation failing with "No account found for
commitment" by replacing `createWithdrawalSecrets` (which requires the
commitment to exist in the calling account's `poolAccounts`) with the
standalone `generateWithdrawalSecrets` SDK function that derives secrets
directly from master keys + label + index.
- Extract the safe account's master keys once before the proof loop and
pass them to `generateWithdrawalSecrets(safeMasterKeys,
commitment.label, 0n)`, matching the SDK's own
`_discoverMigratedCommitments` logic (safe keys at withdrawal index 0).

## Context

Migration crosses account boundaries: commitments live in the **legacy**
account, but new secrets must be derived from the **safe/new** master
keys for key rotation. The previous code called
`createWithdrawalSecrets(accountService, commitment)` on the new
account, which internally searches its (empty) `poolAccounts` and
throws.

fix: fetch Brevis ASP leaves for BSC pools (#21)

In `src/migration/utils/asp.ts`, the `fetchMerkleLeaves` function
previously only fetched Brevis ASP leaves when the specific pool had
`externalAsp` configured. The BNB pool on BSC doesn't have this config,
but its on-chain ASP tree includes Brevis-reviewed deposits. The
generated root from only 0xBow leaves didn't match the `mtRoot` (which
reflects the full on-chain tree), causing the mismatch error.

chain for any Brevis `externalAsp` config. If the pool itself doesn't
have one but a sibling does, that Brevis URL is used to fetch and merge
leaves -- since the Brevis `/leaves` endpoint is not pool-scoped. This
mirrors the chain-level approach used in `useWithdraw.ts`.

fix: use standalone secret derivation for migration proof generation (#14)

## Summary

- Fix migration proof generation failing with "No account found for
commitment" by replacing `createWithdrawalSecrets` (which requires the
commitment to exist in the calling account's `poolAccounts`) with the
standalone `generateWithdrawalSecrets` SDK function that derives secrets
directly from master keys + label + index.
- Extract the safe account's master keys once before the proof loop and
pass them to `generateWithdrawalSecrets(safeMasterKeys,
commitment.label, 0n)`, matching the SDK's own
`_discoverMigratedCommitments` logic (safe keys at withdrawal index 0).

## Context

Migration crosses account boundaries: commitments live in the **legacy**
account, but new secrets must be derived from the **safe/new** master
keys for key rotation. The previous code called
`createWithdrawalSecrets(accountService, commitment)` on the new
account, which internally searches its (empty) `poolAccounts` and
throws.

* feat: add security measures for wallet-based key generation

Implement comprehensive security checks and safeguards for wallet-based
seedphrase generation to prevent non-deterministic signature issues and
ensure users have backup access to their funds.

Changes:
- Add double-signature verification to detect non-deterministic wallets
before generating seedphrase
- Block Coinbase Wallet from wallet-based generation (passkey support
causes non-deterministic signatures)
- Block smart contract wallets (Safe, unknown contracts) except MetaMask
Smart Account (EIP-7702 based, still deterministic)
- Restrict WalletConnect to whitelisted wallets only (MetaMask, Rabby,
Rainbow, Family) to prevent unknown passkey-based wallets
- Implement mandatory seedphrase download flow with disabled continue
button until backup is saved
- Add comprehensive warnings about wallet upgrade/change risks that could
cause loss of access
- Display critical alerts explaining that seedphrase is the ONLY recovery
method if wallet signing method changes

Security rationale:
Wallet-based key generation depends on deterministic signatures. If a
wallet provider updates their signing implementation (e.g., adds nonces,
switches to passkeys, upgrades to smart contract), users would lose
access to their Privacy Pools account. This change ensures users are
aware of these risks and have a recovery backup before proceeding.

**Privacy Score Calculation:**
Privacy score is calculated from three key factors:
1. Total funds (USD value): Position on $0-$100M scale determines base score
2. Anonymity set size: Deposit count on logarithmic scale (1-1000 deposits)
 - More deposits = better privacy (harder to link transactions)

 - Analyzes recent deposit events to calculate coefficient of variation
 - More uniform deposits = better privacy (harder to fingerprint users)
 - Score range: 0.1 (high variance) to 1.0 (very uniform)

The final privacy multiplier combines anonymity and uniformity scores equally,

**Privacy Score Calculation:**
Privacy score is calculated from three key factors:

- Lazy SDK Loading (src/utils/sdk.ts): Circuits only initialized when proof generation functions are called, with client-side only initialization
- Web Worker Infrastructure (src/workers/zkProofWorker.ts, src/hooks/useZKProofWorker.ts): Ready for future use with proper error handling
- Circuit Preloader (src/hooks/useCircuitPreloader.ts, src/providers/CircuitProvider.tsx): Background optimization system
- Enhanced UI (src/containers/Modals/GeneratingZkProof/Generating.tsx): Improved progress indicators with phase tracking
- Sentry Filtering (src/instrumentation-client.ts): Prevents performance alerts from being reported as bugs

User Experience Improvements:
- Users see detailed progress indicators instead of hanging UI during proof generation
- First-time users benefit from background circuit preloading for faster subsequent operations
- Large ZK proof artifacts no longer block the main thread during app initialization
- No more false performance alerts cluttering Sentry reports

* Release v1.1.0 (#66)

* fix: Resolve React DOM manipulation and event decoding errors (#56)

* fix: Resolve React DOM manipulation and event decoding errors

- Replace direct DOM manipulation in AnimatedTree with React state
- Fix event log decoding by silently ignoring non-matching logs

The AnimatedTree component was causing "removeChild" errors by directly
manipulating DOM elements via classList operations while React was managing
the same elements. Replaced with useState-based animation control and proper
cleanup to prevent state updates on unmounted components (sentry error
https://0xbow.sentry.io/issues/6725818367/events/513ba66ea81f44bf9fdeb55facef6419/)

Event decoding was failing when trying to decode all transaction logs using
a specific event ABI. Updated to silently ignore logs that don't match the
expected signature instead of throwing errors.

* fix: Prevent clipboard permission denials from being sent to Sentry

Add error handling to all navigator.clipboard operations to filter out
NotAllowedError exceptions when users deny clipboard permissions. These
are expected user behaviors, not bugs that need tracking.

* fix: Filter wallet provider errors from Sentry reports

Add beforeSend filter to prevent "disconnect is not a function" errors
from being reported to Sentry. These errors occur when users don't have
wallet extensions installed or deny wallet connections, which is expected
user behavior rather than application bugs.

* fix: build error

* fix: Prevent wallet rejection errors from being sent to Sentry

Add filtering for user wallet rejections (UserRejectedRequestError, code 4001)
across all error reporting locations:
- Global beforeSend filter in Sentry client config
- Local filters in useWithdraw and useExit hooks

These are expected user behaviors when users cancel/reject wallet transactions,
not application bugs that need tracking.

* fix: Filter wallet popup failures from Sentry reports

Add filtering for "Pop up window failed to open" errors from Coinbase Wallet SDK.
These errors occur when popup blockers are enabled, users close popups early,
or browser security settings prevent popups - all expected user behaviors
rather than application bugs.

* fix: Implement comprehensive wallet error filtering for Sentry

Add extensive filtering for wallet SDK errors that represent expected user
behavior rather than application bugs:

- User rejections (codes 4001, 4100, 4200)
- JSON-RPC user behavior errors (-32002, -32003, -32603)
- Wallet provider issues (no wallet, popups blocked)
- Chain switching rejections
- WalletConnect user actions (sessions expired, QR closed)
- Network/connection timeouts
- Mobile/browser wallet compatibility issues
- Transaction cancellations by user

Applied filtering across global Sentry config and useWithdraw/useExit hooks
to prevent noise from expected wallet interactions and focus on real bugs.

* fix: Increase transaction timeouts and filter timeout errors from Sentry

Extend viem waitForTransactionReceipt timeouts to handle network congestion:
- Approval transactions: 3 minutes (was ~12 seconds)
- Deposit/withdraw/exit transactions: 5 minutes (was ~12 seconds)

Add WaitForTransactionReceiptTimeoutError to Sentry filters as these are
network/congestion issues rather than application bugs.

Privacy pool transactions can be complex and slow networks need more time
for ZK proof verification and processing.

* fix: Add proactive notification for deposit indexer sync delays

Show informative message after successful deposits to set user expectations
about potential indexer delays when refreshing the page. Includes transaction
hash for verification and reassures users their funds are safe on-chain.

This addresses user confusion when deposits don't appear immediately after
page refresh due to backend/ASP indexer sync delays, not blockchain issues.

* feat: Implement ZK proof performance optimizations

This commit addresses performance issues with large ZK proof artifacts (17MB files causing "Large Render Blocking Asset" Sentry alerts) by implementing lazy loading, preloading strategies, and enhanced progress indicators.

Sentry related issue: https://0xbow.sentry.io/issues/6727590243

Performance Optimizations:
- Lazy Loading: Modified SDK initialization to only load ZK circuits when needed, preventing blocking during app startup
- Web Worker Support: Implemented Web Worker architecture for ZK proof generation to prevent UI blocking (infrastructure ready for future use)
- Circuit Preloading: Added background circuit preloading 2 seconds after app initialization to improve user experience for first-time users
- Enhanced Progress Indicators: Added detailed progress tracking with phase-specific messages (loading circuits, generating proof, verifying proof) and percentage indicators
- Performance Alert Filtering: Added Sentry filtering for "Large Render Blocking Asset" alerts since these are optimization issues, not application bugs

Technical Implementation:
- Lazy SDK Loading (src/utils/sdk.ts): Circuits only initialized when proof generation functions are called, with client-side only initialization
- Web Worker Infrastructure (src/workers/zkProofWorker.ts, src/hooks/useZKProofWorker.ts): Ready for future use with proper error handling
- Circuit Preloader (src/hooks/useCircuitPreloader.ts, src/providers/CircuitProvider.tsx): Background optimization system
- Enhanced UI (src/containers/Modals/GeneratingZkProof/Generating.tsx): Improved progress indicators with phase tracking
- Sentry Filtering (src/instrumentation-client.ts): Prevents performance alerts from being reported as bugs

User Experience Improvements:
- Users see detailed progress indicators instead of hanging UI during proof generation
- First-time users benefit from background circuit preloading for faster subsequent operations
- Large ZK proof artifacts no longer block the main thread during app initialization
- No more false performance alerts cluttering Sentry reports
